But ultimately, A Behanding in Spokane feels as if McDonagh wrote it with one hand tied behind his back.
There's not much to Martin McDonagh's 'A Behanding in Spokane.'
And while I can't exactly say it's a bad play, it's just not a play at all.
Walken is hilarious and the sharply-staged comedy-thriller he haunts packs 90 minutes of nasty entertainment.
Though it offers many laughs and even a suitcase full of severed hands, "Behanding" is surprisingly undeveloped, unedited and lacking in dramatic tension.

cn.t: Walken's magnetic performance energizes McDonagh's darkly comic but ultimately slight and shallow exercise in macabre violence. Critics find it funny yet insubstantial, lacking the depth of the playwright's earlier work.

sg.ra: Shubert/SeatPlan place rows C-E as 'just right' — close enough to catch facial detail without the stage-height skew that rows AA/A suffer inside this shallow 26'9" proscenium house; TickPick singles out row B (seats 105-110) as the best seat in the Schoenfeld.

SeatPlan notes the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but only begins clipping the top of the stage at row Q — so K-P sits in the narrow band that's still unobstructed yet priced below premium; TickPick and Headout independently flag K-P as the value pocket in this 1,079-seat Shubert house.

sg.vl: Overhang cuts the top of the stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly says rows beyond Q lose the top of the stage to the mezzanine overhang, and Headout/TickPick corroborate that under-overhang seats 'might have obstructed views from the overhang of the box seats or the mezzanine itself' — a real issue in this shallow Shubert house where the mezz projects forward.

sg.vl: Overhead sweep of the whole stage
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both cite front center mezz rows A-B as offering 'excellent overhead views perfect for appreciating the stage in one sweep' — the Schoenfeld's mezz hangs closer to the stage than larger Shubert houses, so row A feels surprisingly close rather than distant.

SeatPlan flags E-G as benefiting from 'great rake for aerial views which cover the entire stage below' — the Schoenfeld mezz is steeper than most Shubert houses, so E-G keeps the full stage visible where a flatter rake would start clipping; Headout calls it a value tier below the premium A-D band.

Multiple sources describe rear mezz past row F as 'a gamble... actors start to look like LEGO figures' — despite the Schoenfeld only having 392 mezz seats, the steep rake trades sightline for proximity and you lose emotional read on faces; a J104 reviewer conceded 'nearly center, no obstructions' but 2nd-to-last row.

SeatPlan notes 'single-digit seats in rows A-D' of the side mezz 'are more directly above the stage and feel surprisingly close' — the Schoenfeld's narrow 40-foot proscenium means side-mezz angles are less punishing than wider houses, though TickPick warns the far edges of rows 'have slightly blocked views of the corners of the stage'.
